impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's application of its Penumbra precedent—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis applies only to pre-AIA law and not to prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—was correct when determining the effective filing date of a reference patent based on its provisional application.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that challenged patent claims were unpatentable as obvious, disagreeing with the Board's approach under Penumbra for determining when a reference patent qualifies as prior art under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court remanded for further consideration of whether the Carrier reference was entitled to its provisional application filing date. This decision is significant because it directly impacts how the PTAB evaluates the prior art status of patent references with provisional applications under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially narrower scope of prior art available in IPR proceedings, as challengers may face a higher burden to establish that a reference patent is entitled to its provisional application's filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2).
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR petitions to invalidate competitors' patents may find it harder to use reference patents as prior art when the reference's relevant subject matter may not be fully supported by its provisional application's written description.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages against the government, and what constitutes a permissible application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in hypothetical negotiation damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software, rejecting the argument that damages must be anchored to an existing license agreement. However, the court vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom and assessed non-compensatory damages. This case provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government software procurement contexts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's affirmation that damages are not capped by pre-existing license rates, allowing for potentially higher recovery in infringement cases where the government exceeds license terms.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur on the book of wisdom issue signals that courts must be more careful in damages calculations, potentially complicating future damages presentations for copyright holders seeking to recover beyond contractual rates.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether Ford was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case provides significant guidance on trade secret damages methodologies and the standard for excluding damages expert testimony under Daubert.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies asserting trade secret claims benefit from the court's instruction to reconsider previously excluded damages models, potentially broadening the range of acceptable approaches for quantifying trade secret misappropriation damages. The reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award also supports deference to jury findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation face continued exposure as the court affirmed liability, and the remand for reconsideration of damages models could result in larger awards than the district court originally permitted.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems claim patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied judgment as a matter of law on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims related to non-uniform constellation designs for communication systems while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The court's split treatment of eligibility across related patents in the same family provides important guidance on how courts should assess § 101 eligibility for technology standards-related patents. The case involved a substantial jury verdict against LG for willful infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in telecommunications and standards-essential technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and the preservation of the infringement and damages verdicts, supporting enforcement of technology standards patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the vacatur of eligibility for some claims creates uncertainty about the scope of § 101 protection for standards-related inventions requiring further proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to enforcement-only activities constituted a cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement conveyed all substantial rights to TexasLDPC, entitling it to sue for patent and copyright infringement without joining the university patent owner. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to an enforcement-focused business model did not constitute a cessation of business operations under the agreement. This decision clarifies the standing requirements for exclusive licensees and validates enforcement-focused licensing entities.
impacts.positiveImplications: University technology transfer programs and exclusive licensees benefit from clearer guidance that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can convey standing to sue without joining the licensor, and that enforcement-focused business models are legitimate under license agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on the non-joinder of the patent owner when the exclusive license conveys all substantial rights, and cannot argue that a licensee's pivot to enforcement constitutes a terminating cessation of business.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation as referring to salt forms rather than free base forms, and whether the district court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic version of Nuedexta, upholding the district court's claim construction of pharmaceutical compound terms in the weight-to-weight ratio limitation. However, the court vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. This decision has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent litigation and generic drug market entry timing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction blocking generic competition, preserving market exclusivity until patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face delayed market entry, and the bond requirement vacatur means brand-name companies must post security when obtaining preliminary injunctions, adding financial risk to enforcement efforts.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patents directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding infringement and validity of UT's patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions used in coronary stents, holding that BSC was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court did not reach UT's cross-appeal on willfulness. This decision eliminates a significant damages award against BSC and provides guidance on anticipation analysis for composition-of-matter claims in the medical device field.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the reversal, which removes infringement liability and provides a defense framework for anticipation challenges to university-held patents covering implant compositions.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and technology transfer offices face increased risk that jury verdicts in their favor may be overturned on JMOL, particularly where prior art arguably discloses the claimed compositions.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit should rehear en banc the question of whether Egyptian Goddess improperly shifted the design patent infringement inquiry to focus on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction of design patents involves factual questions of functionality that should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc on a design patent infringement case, with a divided court issuing separate concurring and dissenting opinions. The dissent argued that the Egyptian Goddess framework has improperly allowed courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment based on differences rather than overall similarity, and that functionality determinations should go to a jury. This denial preserves the current framework but signals potential instability in design patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against design patent claims benefit from the preservation of the current Egyptian Goddess framework, which allows summary judgment of non-infringement when designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued challenges at summary judgment, and the strong dissent signals that the current infringement test may be revisited in the future, creating uncertainty for design patent enforcement strategies.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement provision requiring payment 'if any Asserted Claim survives the EPR,' or whether the dispute is a state-law contract interpretation question belonging in a regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit, holding that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the dispute over whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination was fundamentally a state-law contract interpretation question that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. This decision has important implications for jurisdictional routing of patent settlement agreement disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement disputes face jurisdictional uncertainty, as disputes over settlement agreement terms tied to patent proceedings may not be heard in the Federal Circuit, potentially leading to less specialized adjudication and inconsistent outcomes across regional circuits.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling from a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. The case involved bank holding company claims for breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings arising from the 2008 financial crisis and government conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. This ruling eliminates American Pipe tolling as a tool for plaintiffs bringing Tucker Act claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from a firm statute of limitations defense against stale claims in the Court of Federal Claims, providing greater certainty and finality in financial crisis-related litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors who relied on class action tolling to preserve individual claims against the government face the permanent loss of those claims if the limitations period has expired, particularly affecting those harmed by the 2008 financial crisis and GSE conservatorship.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulatory 15-day filing deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews was a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority, even though the statute imposed no express deadline. The court found the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking within the bounds of the agency's power. This decision preserves Commerce's procedural framework for sunset reviews that can lead to revocation of antidumping duty orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers benefit from a clear procedural framework, as domestic competitors who fail to respond within 15 days may see antidumping duty orders revoked, potentially reducing trade barriers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic manufacturers relying on antidumping duty protection face a strict 15-day deadline to participate in sunset reviews, and failure to meet this deadline could result in revocation of protective duty orders.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salts, pharmaceutical formulations thereof, and methods of treating cancer therewith satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of three patents covering crystalline forms of the cancer drug cabozantinib malate (the active ingredient in Cabometyx®) had adequate written description support. The court dismissed the appeal as to a fourth patent's claim. This decision preserves Exelixis's patent protection for a blockbuster cancer drug and provides guidance on written description requirements for crystalline polymorph patents in pharmaceutical litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for crystalline salt form patents, supporting the enforceability of patents protecting commercially significant drugs and their formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the court's affirmance sustains patent exclusivity through 2030.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether 'executable program code' limitations in software patent claims should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether § 112(f) applies to 'executable program code' claim limitations, in light of the intervening Dyfan precedent. The court affirmed the judgment of invalidity for anticipation on the '638 patent. This decision is significant for software patent prosecution and litigation, as it may narrow when § 112(f) is triggered for software-implemented claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue against § 112(f) treatment of 'executable program code' limitations under updated precedent, potentially rescuing claims previously held indefinite.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent claims face uncertainty as previously invalidated claims may be revived on remand under the Dyfan framework.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may reach the merits of a Rule 12(b)(6) patent eligibility dismissal after already concluding that venue is improper and dismissing under Rule 12(b)(3).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent-ineligibility grounds, holding that there is no legal prohibition against a court addressing a Rule 12(b)(6) motion after granting dismissal for improper venue. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was found ineligible under § 101. This decision clarifies that courts may issue merits rulings alongside venue dismissals, potentially creating preclusive effects.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain both venue and merits-based dismissals in a single motion, potentially creating issue-preclusive effects that prevent re-filing in proper venues.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders filing in questionable venues risk not only dismissal for improper venue but also a simultaneous adverse ruling on patent eligibility that could bar future litigation of the same claims.
